claim: Ocular position exhibits continuous slow changes, often referred to as drifts, when microsaccades are not occurring during maintained gaze fixation.
source: When microsaccades are not occurring, ocular position exhibits continuous slow changes, often referred to as drifts.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known property of fixational eye movements.

claim: Drifts remain to be viewed as largely random eye movements, unlike microsaccades.
source: Unlike microsaccades, drifts remain to be viewed as largely random eye movements.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field as described in the abstract.

claim: Fleeting (~8 ms duration) stimulus presentations can robustly trigger transient and stimulus-specific modulations of ocular position drifts with approximately 60 ms latency.
source: We used highly precise eye tracking in three well trained macaque monkeys and found that even fleeting (~8 ms duration) stimulus presentations can robustly trigger transient and stimulus-specific modulations of ocular position drifts, and with only approximately 60 ms latency.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental data from three monkeys.

claim: Drift responses are binocular.
source: Such drift responses are binocular, and they are most effectively elicited with large stimuli of low spatial frequency.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the experiments.

claim: Drift responses are most effectively elicited with large stimuli of low spatial frequency.
source: Such drift responses are binocular, and they are most effectively elicited with large stimuli of low spatial frequency.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the experiments.

claim: The drift responses exhibit some image pattern selectivity.
source: Intriguingly, the drift responses exhibit some image pattern selectivity, and they are not explained by convergence responses, pupil constrictions, head movements, or starting eye positions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the experiments.

claim: The drift responses are not explained by convergence responses.
source: Intriguingly, the drift responses exhibit some image pattern selectivity, and they are not explained by convergence responses, pupil constrictions, head movements, or starting eye positions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from control experiments.

claim: The drift responses are not explained by pupil constrictions.
source: Intriguingly, the drift responses exhibit some image pattern selectivity, and they are not explained by convergence responses, pupil constrictions, head movements, or starting eye positions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from control experiments.

claim: The drift responses are not explained by head movements.
source: Intriguingly, the drift responses exhibit some image pattern selectivity, and they are not explained by convergence responses, pupil constrictions, head movements, or starting eye positions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from control experiments.

claim: The drift responses are not explained by starting eye positions.
source: Intriguingly, the drift responses exhibit some image pattern selectivity, and they are not explained by convergence responses, pupil constrictions, head movements, or starting eye positions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from control experiments.

claim: Ocular position drifts have very rapid access to exogenous visual information.
source: Ocular position drifts have very rapid access to exogenous visual information.
evidence: This is the concluding statement of the abstract, summarizing the main finding.

claim: Eye position changes subtly even when perfect gaze fixation is attempted.
source: Eye position changes subtly even when perfect gaze fixation is attempted (Barlow, 1952; Nachmias, 1959; Nachmias, 1961; Ratliff and Riggs, 1950; Steinman et al., 1973).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Fixational eye movement comes in two primary flavors: microsaccades and ocular position drifts.
source: Such 'fixational' eye movement comes in two primary flavors: microsaccades, which resemble large saccades (Hafed, 2011; Rolfs, 2009; Zuber et al., 1965) and rapidly shift gaze position by a minute amount; and ocular position drifts, which are even smaller and slower eye movements (Barlow, 1952; Ditchburn and Ginsborg, 1953; Martins et al., 1985; Nachmias, 1959; Nachmias, 1961; Poletti and Rucci, 2016; Ratliff and Riggs, 1950; Skinner et al., 2019; St Cyr and Fender, 1969).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Microsaccades resemble large saccades and rapidly shift gaze position by a minute amount.
source: microsaccades, which resemble large saccades (Hafed, 2011; Rolfs, 2009; Zuber et al., 1965) and rapidly shift gaze position by a minute amount
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Ocular position drifts are even smaller and slower eye movements than microsaccades.
source: ocular position drifts, which are even smaller and slower eye movements (Barlow, 1952; Ditchburn and Ginsborg, 1953; Martins et al., 1985; Nachmias, 1959; Nachmias, 1961; Poletti and Rucci, 2016; Ratliff and Riggs, 1950; Skinner et al., 2019; St Cyr and Fender, 1969).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Microsaccades are not random but are very systematically influenced by peripheral as well as foveal visual stimuli.
source: Despite contrary ideas in the past century, a now accepted property of microsaccades is that, like larger saccades, they are not random but are very systematically (Engbert, 2006; Engbert and Kliegl, 2003; Hafed and Clark, 2002; Hafed and Ignashchenkova, 2013; Hafed et al., 2011; Ko et al., 2010; Rolfs et al., 2008; Thaler et al., 2013; Tian et al., 2016) and rapidly (Buonocore et al., 2017a; Hafed and Ignashchenkova, 2013; Rolfs et al., 2008; Tian et al., 2016; Tian et al., 2018) influenced by peripheral as well as foveal visual stimuli, among other factors (Hafed et al., 2015; Willeke et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Microsaccades are rapidly influenced by peripheral as well as foveal visual stimuli.
source: Despite contrary ideas in the past century, a now accepted property of microsaccades is that, like larger saccades, they are not random but are very systematically (Engbert, 2006; Engbert and Kliegl, 2003; Hafed and Clark, 2002; Hafed and Ignashchenkova, 2013; Hafed et al., 2011; Ko et al., 2010; Rolfs et al., 2008; Thaler et al., 2013; Tian et al., 2016) and rapidly (Buonocore et al., 2017a; Hafed and Ignashchenkova, 2013; Rolfs et al., 2008; Tian et al., 2016; Tian et al., 2018) influenced by peripheral as well as foveal visual stimuli, among other factors (Hafed et al., 2015; Willeke et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The brain mechanisms for controlling ocular position drifts are unknown.
source: In stark contrast, the brain mechanisms for controlling ocular position drifts are unknown; these movements continue to be thought of as random, often being modeled as random walk processes (Burak et al., 2010; Engbert and Kliegl, 2004; Engbert et al., 2011; Herrmann et al., 2017; Kuang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as the current state of knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Ocular position drifts continue to be thought of as random, often being modeled as random walk processes.
source: these movements continue to be thought of as random, often being modeled as random walk processes (Burak et al., 2010; Engbert and Kliegl, 2004; Engbert et al., 2011; Herrmann et al., 2017; Kuang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Slow ocular position drifts exhibit behavioral characteristics supporting some level of central nervous system control over them.
source: This is despite the fact that slow ocular position drifts exhibit behavioral characteristics (e.g. Ditchburn and Ginsborg, 1953; Nachmias, 1961) supporting some level of central nervous system control over them.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Ocular position drifts aid in stabilizing eye position near a certain location.
source: For example, these eye movements aid in stabilizing eye position near a certain location (e.g. Epelboim and Kowler, 1993)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Ocular position drifts can compensate for subtle head movements through mechanisms likely related to the vestibular ocular reflex.
source: they can compensate for subtle head movements through mechanisms likely related to the vestibular ocular reflex (e.g. Ditchburn and Ginsborg, 1953; Poletti et al., 2015; Schor and Westall, 1984; Skavenski et al., 1979; Steinman and Collewijn, 1980)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Ocular position drifts appear to be associated with internal knowledge of their occurrence for regulating the perception (or lack thereof) of the image motions that they cause on the retina.
source: and they also appear to be associated with internal knowledge of their occurrence for regulating the perception (or lack thereof) of the image motions that they cause on the retina (e.g. Poletti et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Ocular position drifts can exhibit highly systematic stimulus-driven modulations in both speed and direction.
source: Here, we used precise eye tracking in three well trained rhesus macaque monkeys to demonstrate that ocular position drifts can exhibit highly systematic stimulus-driven modulations in both speed and direction.
evidence: This is stated as a primary finding from the experiments.

claim: The stimulus-driven modulations of ocular position drifts have a very short latency.
source: These modulations have a very short latency, and they are stimulus-tuned and binocular.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the experiments.

claim: The stimulus-driven modulations of ocular position drifts are stimulus-tuned.
source: These modulations have a very short latency, and they are stimulus-tuned and binocular.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the experiments.

claim: The stimulus-driven modulations of ocular position drifts are independent of head movements, convergence responses, and starting eye positions.
source: These modulations are also independent of head movements, convergence responses, and starting eye positions.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from control experiments.

claim: The amplitudes of the drift response are sufficient to move images across individual cone photoreceptors in the fovea or multiple rod photoreceptors in some peripheral zones.
source: Moreover, their amplitudes are sufficient to move images across individual cone photoreceptors in the fovea or multiple rod photoreceptors in some peripheral zones.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the measured amplitudes and known photoreceptor spacing.

claim: In monkey A, the upward velocity pulse started at ~80 ms and lasted for ~60 ms.
source: In monkey A, the upward velocity pulse started at ~80 ms and lasted for ~60 ms (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a specific measurement from the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In monkey M, the upward velocity pulse started at ~60 ms and lasted for ~90 ms.
source: These values were ~60 ms and ~90 ms, respectively, for monkey M (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is a specific measurement from the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In monkey N, the upward velocity pulse started at ~70 ms and lasted for ~100 ms.
source: and ~70 ms and ~100 ms, respectively, for monkey N (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is a specific measurement from the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: In all three monkeys, the drift response consisted of a predominantly upward velocity pulse reaching a peak speed of ~33–45 min arc/s, or ~0.55–0.75 deg/s.
source: In all three monkeys, the drift response consisted of a predominantly upward velocity pulse reaching a peak speed of ~33–45 min arc/s, or ~0.55–0.75 deg/s (Figure 1B,D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,D,H,J)
evidence: This is a measurement from the data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: In all three monkeys, the drift response resulted in a displacement of ~2–3 min arc, or 0.034–0.05 deg.
source: and a resultant displacement of ~2–3 min arc, or 0.034–0.05 deg (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,G).
evidence: This is a measurement from the data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Foveal cone photoreceptor separation in the rhesus macaque retina is ~1 min arc.
source: For example, foveal cone photoreceptor separation in the rhesus macaque retina is ~1 min arc (Rolls and Cowey, 1970)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Rod photoreceptor density can be even higher in the rod peak region than cone photoreceptor density in the fovea.
source: and rod photoreceptor density can be even higher in the rod peak region (Wikler et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The stimulus-driven drift response clearly modulates input images to the visual system.
source: Thus, the stimulus-driven drift response clearly modulates input images to the visual system.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured displacement and known photoreceptor spacing.

claim: The drift response was transient: when considering longer periods of saccade-free fixation, the eye velocity 'pulse' subsided, and eye position reverted back to its steady-state drift direction.
source: The drift response was also transient: when we considered longer periods of saccade-free fixation, we did not notice increasing durations of drift response. Instead, the eye velocity 'pulse' subsided, and eye position reverted back to its steady-state drift direction that was prominent, and stereotyped, in each monkey (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,J).
evidence: This is a finding from the data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The horizontal component of the eye movement during the drift pulse was systematically biased by the side of darkness in all three monkeys.
source: In all three monkeys, the horizontal component of the eye movement during the drift pulse was systematically biased by the side of darkness (Figure 1E,F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F,K,L): the upward drift tilted rightward when the darkness was on the right of gaze and leftward when it was on the left, and these results were statistically significant (pink intervals on all relevant x-axes of plots; Methods).
evidence: This is a finding from the data shown in the referenced figures, with statistical significance.

claim: The upward drift tilted rightward when the darkness was on the right of gaze and leftward when it was on the left.
source: the upward drift tilted rightward when the darkness was on the right of gaze and leftward when it was on the left, and these results were statistically significant (pink intervals on all relevant x-axes of plots; Methods).
evidence: This is a finding from the data with statistical significance.

claim: The horizontal component of eye position reacted to the spatial position of the luminance transient.
source: The horizontal component of eye position therefore reacted to the spatial position of the luminance transient.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed horizontal bias as a function of stimulus side.

claim: The horizontal bias as a function of stimulus appearance occurred regardless of whether the right or left eye was tracked.
source: However, this is unlikely to explain our observations: the horizontal bias as a function of stimulus appearance (e.g. Figure 1E,F) occurred regardless of whether we tracked the right (monkeys M and N) or left (monkey A) eye.
evidence: This is a finding from the data that rules out convergence as an explanation.

claim: Pupillary responses to stimulus transients exhibit significantly slower dynamics than the drift response.
source: Moreover, pupillary responses to stimulus transients exhibit significantly slower dynamics (Clarke et al., 2003; Pong and Fuchs, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The pupillary constriction caused by stimulus onset occurred later than the ocular position drift response.
source: Using a stimulus manipulation in which the upward drift response was clearly visible in the (left) eye (tracked with a scleral search coil), simultaneous measurement of pupil diameter in the other eye (tracked with a video-based eye tracker; Methods) revealed that the pupillary constriction caused by stimulus onset occurred later than the ocular position drift response (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the control experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Video-based eye trackers are not capable of resolving the drift response.
source: It was futile to look for the drift response in the right eye, confirming that video-based eye trackers are not capable of resolving such small detail (Choe et al., 2016; Kimmel et al., 2012; Wyatt, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and confirmed by the authors' observations.

claim: The drift response occurred in both eyes simultaneously.
source: Importantly, the drift response occurred in both eyes simultaneously (Figure 2A,C)
evidence: This is a finding from the binocular tracking experiment shown in Figure 2A,C.

claim: The horizontal component of eye position did not show an appreciable convergence response of similar magnitude to the drift response.
source: and the horizontal component of eye position did not show an appreciable convergence response of similar magnitude (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: This is a finding from the binocular tracking experiment shown in Figure 2B,D.

claim: In the time interval capturing the drift response (50–140 ms), there was no statistically significant difference between right and left peak vertical or peak horizontal eye velocity.
source: We confirmed this statistically; in a time interval capturing the drift response (50–140 ms), there was no statistically significant difference between right and left peak vertical or peak horizontal eye velocity (p=0.249, Z = 1.15 for vertical and p=0.8321, Z = 0.21 for horizontal; Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the binocular tracking data.

claim: The stimulus-driven drift response is a binocular eye movement phenomenon that is independent of a convergence response.
source: Therefore, the stimulus-driven drift response (Figures 1 and 2) is a binocular eye movement phenomenon that is independent of a convergence response.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the binocular tracking data and statistical analysis.

claim: When the flash was switched to white, the drift response still occurred.
source: When we switched the flash to white (reddish curve), the drift response still occurred.
evidence: This is a finding from the experiment comparing black and white flashes.

claim: Peak eye velocity was significantly higher with black than white flashes in both monkeys.
source: Statistically, peak eye velocity was significantly higher with black than white flashes in both monkeys (p=4.2×10−14, Z = 7.55 for monkey A and p=4.3×10−5, Z = 4.09 for monkey M; Wilcoxon rank sum test)
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the data comparing black and white flashes.

claim: The drift response is not part of a near reflex triad (convergence, accommodation, and pupil constriction).
source: We considered the possibility that the stimulus-driven drift response was part of a near reflex triad (convergence, accommodation, and pupil constriction) (Myers and Stark, 1990; Nachmias, 1961). For example, the luminance transient may have been perceived by the monkey as a change in depth plane. However, this is unlikely to explain our observations
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the binocular tracking data and other control experiments.

claim: The drift response was not accompanied by a head movement.
source: For all three sets of new experiments, we replicated the drift response observation in the same monkey (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A). Simultaneous measurements of head position (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C) did not reveal any concomitant head movements.
evidence: This is a finding from the control experiment with simultaneous eye and head tracking.

claim: For eye movements, there was a significant difference between vertical eye velocity during the post-stimulus drift interval and the pre-stimulus baseline interval.
source: For eye movements, there was a significant difference between vertical eye velocity during the post-stimulus drift interval and the pre-stimulus baseline interval (p=5.55×10−19 and Z = −8.9, p=3.27×10−18 and Z = −8.7, p=1.05×10−13 and Z = −7.44, respectively, for the three head coil positions in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the eye movement data from the head tracking experiment.

claim: For head movements, none of the head coil positions tested resulted in substantial movements after stimulus onset.
source: For head movements, none of the head coil positions that we tested resulted in substantial movements after stimulus onset (p=0.1394 to 0.8911 and Z = −0.91 to 1.48 across all positions and channels in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C; Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the head movement data from the head tracking experiment.

claim: The head did not move at the same time as the ocular position drift response, ruling out both a compensatory eye movement explanation as well as an artifactual change in sensed position due to displacement of the eye's 3-dimensional position in the search coil system's magnetic fields.
source: These results mean that the head did not move at the same time as the ocular position drift response, ruling out both a compensatory eye movement explanation as well as an artifactual change in sensed position due to displacement of the eye's 3-dimensional position in the search coil system's magnetic fields.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the head tracking data and statistical analysis.

claim: A significant swath (i.e. low spatial frequency) of luminance transience seemed necessary for the drift response.
source: A significant swath (i.e. low spatial frequency) of luminance transience seemed necessary for the drift response. We did not observe the short-latency response as strongly with small localized targets briefly flashed to the right or left of fixation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiment comparing full-screen and localized flashes.

claim: The ocular position drift response exhibited clear preference for low spatial frequencies in both response latency and magnitude.
source: We saw clear preference for low spatial frequencies in the drift response, both in response latency and magnitude (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial frequency tuning experiment shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There was an effect of spatial frequency on both peak velocity and peak velocity latency.
source: There was an effect of spatial frequency on both peak velocity (p=2.2×10−16, χ2(4)=79.49) and peak velocity latency (p=3.1×10−17, χ2(4)=83.56).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the spatial frequency tuning data.

claim: The drift response was earliest and strongest for the lowest spatial frequency.
source: Post-hoc tests revealed that the drift response was earliest (adjusted p<9.3×10−8 against all other spatial frequencies) and strongest (adjusted p<0.0021 against the third to fifth spatial frequencies) for the lowest spatial frequency.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the spatial frequency tuning data.

claim: When grating orientation was varied rather than spatial frequency, the drift response was again altered and displayed a form of orientation tuning.
source: In fact, when we ran yet another experiment with grating orientation, rather than spatial frequency, the drift response of the same monkey was again altered, and it displayed a form of orientation tuning (Figure 3B; p=0.01, χ2(4)=11.0 for peak velocity and p=0.0004, χ2(4)=18.5 for peak velocity latency; Kruskal-Wallis test).
evidence: This is a finding from the orientation tuning experiment shown in Figure 3B, with statistical analysis.

claim: Ocular position drifts are sensitive, with short latency, to stimulus transients and their image features.
source: Thus, ocular position drifts are sensitive, with short latency, to stimulus transients and their image features.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the spatial frequency and orientation tuning experiments.

claim: The drift response occurred when it was least likely to observe microsaccades.
source: The drift response occurred when it was least likely to observe microsaccades.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis relating drift response timing to microsaccade rate.

claim: Saccade and microsaccade likelihood decreases dramatically shortly after visual transients.
source: Specifically, it was long known that saccade and microsaccade likelihood decreases dramatically shortly after visual transients (Buonocore et al., 2017a; Buonocore and McIntosh, 2008; Edelman and Xu, 2009; Engbert and Kliegl, 2003; Hafed and Ignashchenkova, 2013; Hafed et al., 2011; Reingold and Stampe, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The stimulus dependence of the ocular drift response and its timing relative to saccadic inhibition suggest that the ocular drift response is mechanistically linked to the circuits mediating saccadic inhibition.
source: The stimulus dependence of the ocular drift response (e.g. Figure 3) and its timing relative to saccadic inhibition (and indeed relative to the timing of early sensory responses in the oculomotor system; Chen et al., 2018) suggest that the ocular drift response is mechanistically linked to the circuits mediating saccadic inhibition; and particularly to the short-latency visual responses in these circuits.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing relationships observed in the data.

claim: Stimulus onset triggers both saccadic inhibition and drift response.
source: That is, stimulus onset triggers both saccadic inhibition and drift response.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing relationships observed in the data.

claim: The drift response could still occur with nearby microsaccades before or after it.
source: Moreover, we found that the drift response could still occur with nearby microsaccades before or after it.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of trials with microsaccades near the drift response.

claim: The amplitude of the drift response seemed similar regardless of the timing of nearby microsaccades.
source: Interestingly, the amplitude of the drift response seemed similar regardless of the timing of nearby microsaccades (Figure 4G–I).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 4G–I.

claim: The same upward drift response was present with different starting eye positions.
source: Finally, we checked whether the drift response could still occur with different starting eye positions. We divided trials based on eye position being above or below median vertical eye position across trials (Methods), and the same upward drift response was present (Figure 2—figure supplement 3 shows these results from the black fixation flash paradigm in monkeys A and M).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The drift response was too small to even elicit corrective downward microsaccades after it occurred: there was no clear bias for downward microsaccades after the drift response.
source: And, the drift response was too small to even elicit corrective downward microsaccades after it occurred: there was no clear bias for downward microsaccades after the drift response (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Slow fixational drift eye movements are systematically influenced by visual transients.
source: Our results demonstrate that slow fixational drift eye movements are systematically influenced by visual transients.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the experimental data.

claim: Classic brainstem neurophysiological studies of the oculomotor system are too coarse to provide the mechanistic insights necessary for explaining the observed drift responses.
source: Classic brainstem neurophysiological studies of the oculomotor system (e.g. reviewed in: Takahashi and Shinoda, 2018) are too coarse to provide the mechanistic insights necessary for explaining our observations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal precision of the observed drift responses.

claim: Visual responses in oculomotor control circuitry likely play a role in the drift response given its temporal transience and dependence on spatial frequency.
source: Given the temporal transience of the drift response and its dependence on spatial frequency, it is likely that visual responses in oculomotor control circuitry play a role.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed properties of the drift response.

claim: Low spatial frequency stimuli may increase the spatial uncertainty of intended gaze position.
source: One possibility is that low spatial frequency stimuli increase the spatial uncertainty of intended gaze position.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: The superior colliculus has overrepresentation of the upper visual field.
source: It is conceivable that such increased uncertainty, coupled with overrepresentation of the upper visual field in the SC (Hafed and Chen, 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Visual bursts for upper visual field locations occur earlier in the superior colliculus.
source: as well as earlier visual bursts for upper visual field locations
evidence: This is stated as a known property of the superior colliculus.

claim: The superior colliculus influences eye position.
source: Indeed, the SC influences eye position (Hafed et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Visual responses in the nucleus raphe interpositus (rip) have been reported in the cat.
source: In the cat, visual responses in the nucleus raphe interpositus (rip) have been reported (Evinger et al., 1982)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: There are hints of visual responses in monkey rip.
source: and there are hints of visual responses in monkey rip (Busettini and Mays, 2003; Everling et al., 1998; Missal and Keller, 2002), although no visual tuning was explicitly investigated.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The superior colliculus projects to brainstem oculomotor control circuits.
source: Given both the preponderance and richness of SC visual responses (e.g. Chen and Hafed, 2018; Chen et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2018), and given the fact that the SC projects to brainstem oculomotor control circuits
evidence: This is stated as a known anatomical fact.

claim: The authors hypothesize the presence of feature-tuned visual responses in brainstem oculomotor control circuits.
source: we hypothesize the presence of feature-tuned visual responses in such oculomotor control circuits.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a hypothesis.

claim: In an earlier human study in which natural images were presented during fixation, drift speeds were notably the highest in the very first analyzed time bin after image onset.
source: Indeed, in an earlier human study in which natural images (rich in low spatial frequency content) were presented during fixation, drift speeds were notably the highest in the very first analyzed time bin after image onset (Poletti, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Saccadic inhibition is thought to reflect a resetting of ongoing saccadic rhythms to enable reacting to the external stimulus arriving asynchronously to such rhythms.
source: Saccadic inhibition is thought to reflect a resetting of ongoing saccadic rhythms to enable reacting (often with a subsequent eye movement) to the external stimulus arriving asynchronously to such rhythms (Buonocore et al., 2017a; Hafed and Ignashchenkova, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The brief period of saccadic inhibition provides an important time window during which perceptual and cognitive processing of the incoming external stimulus could proceed.
source: Increasing behavioral work is also suggesting that the brief period of such saccadic inhibition additionally provides an important time window during which perceptual and cognitive processing of the incoming external stimulus could proceed (Bompas et al., 2020; Buonocore et al., 2017b; Salinas and Stanford, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Different subclasses of visual neurons (e.g. in primary visual cortex) will be differentially activated by different speeds and amplitudes of fixational eye movements.
source: Coupled with evidence that different subclasses of visual neurons (e.g. in primary visual cortex) will be differentially activated by different speeds and amplitudes of fixational eye movements (Snodderly, 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: During smooth pursuit initiation, when the same flash paradigms as in the current study were used, the stimulus onsets consistently reduced smooth eye velocity rather than enhanced it.
source: Indeed, during smooth pursuit initiation (i.e. with very small eye velocities, albeit still faster than the ocular position drifts in our current study), when we used the same flash paradigms as in the current study, we found that the stimulus onsets consistently reduced smooth eye velocity rather than enhanced it (Buonocore et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: A random walk model of ocular position drifts is not necessarily accurate.
source: A strong implication of our work is, then, that a random walk model of ocular position drifts (Burak et al., 2010; Engbert and Kliegl, 2004; Engbert et al., 2011; Herrmann et al., 2017; Kuang et al., 2012) is not necessarily accurate.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Monkey N was 12 years old at the time of the experiments.
source: Monkey N was 12 years old at the time of the experiments
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental subjects.

claim: Monkeys A and M were 6–9 years old at the time of the experiments.
source: monkeys A and M were 6–9 years old.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental subjects.

claim: Each monkey was initially implanted with a titanium head holder under aseptic surgical conditions.
source: Each monkey was initially implanted with a titanium head holder under aseptic surgical conditions, as described earlier (Chen and Hafed, 2013).
